entries.question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
entries.reason: Both conclude that after Lay Claim resolves Analia ends up controlling both Corrupted Conscience and Bane Alley Blackguard, matching the reference's final ruling.
entries.answer:
After Analia's Lay Claim resolves, Analia controls both Corrupted Conscience and Bane Alley Blackguard.

Why: Lay Claim reads "Enchant permanent / You control enchanted permanent," so Analia gains control of Nico's Corrupted Conscience (an Aura is a permanent, so it's a legal target for Lay Claim's enchant ability) [303.4e]. Corrupted Conscience reads "You control enchanted creature" — the "you" in an Aura's text means that Aura's controller at the time the effect is applied, which is now Analia [Lay Claim ruling #0]. So Corrupted Conscience's control-change effect now hands Bane Alley Blackguard to Analia instead of Nico.

Control-changing effects are applied in layer 2 of the layer system, and they're recalculated continuously from the actual objects, so as soon as Analia becomes Corrupted Conscience's controller, Bane Alley Blackguard's controller updates too [613.1b]. Note that Analia is also Bane Alley Blackguard's owner and its default controller, so nothing odd happens even if Corrupted Conscience later leaves the battlefield [110.2].

Also note the general principle in the other direction: gaining control of a creature does not give you control of Auras attached to it, and vice versa [303.4e][Lay Claim ruling #0] — here the control change flows only because Corrupted Conscience's own text grants control to its controller.

This works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; the only multiplayer wrinkle in the provided rules is that if a player leaves the game, control effects they provided end and objects can be exiled or leave the game [800.4a][800.4c]. No timing ambiguity affects the outcome here — I've assumed Lay Claim resolved successfully and both Auras remain on the battlefield.

entries.answer_gold: Analia controls both permanents. Out of the two auras, Corrupted Conscience has the earlier timestamp, and would normally be applied first. However, the effects from both auras apply in the same layer, applying the Lay Claim's effect would change how the Corrupted Conscience's effect is applied, and applying the Corrupted Conscience's effect would not change how the Lay Claim's effect is applied, so the Corrupted Conscience's effect is dependent on the Lay Claim's effect. The Lay Claim's effect applies first, giving Analia control of Corrupted Conscience, and then the Corrupted Conscience's effect applies, giving Analia control of Bane Alley Blackguard.

entries.question: Alan controls [Iroas, God of Victory] and 3 other enchantments. Their devotion to white is 2. They cast [Starfield of Nyx]. After it resolves, is Iroas, God of Victory a creature? If so, what are its power and toughness?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference: Starfield of Nyx makes Iroas a creature and sets its power/toughness to its mana value (4/4).
entries.answer:
Yes — Iroas, God of Victory is a creature after Starfield of Nyx resolves, and it's a 4/4.

Why:

1. Devotion. Devotion to red and white counts mana symbols that are red, white, or both among the mana costs of permanents Alan controls (700.5a). Iroas, God of Victory's own {2}{R}{W} contributes 2, and Alan's devotion to white is 2 — nowhere near seven. Starfield of Nyx costs {4}{W}, adding one white symbol, so devotion to red and white is still well under seven. So Iroas, God of Victory's own ability "As long as your devotion to red and white is less than seven, Iroas isn't a creature" is active. Note devotion is calculated after copy/control/text-changing effects but before other characteristic-modifying effects (700.5a), so Starfield of Nyx's type-changing doesn't alter the count.

2. Layer 4 (types). Two effects apply: Iroas, God of Victory's ability removing the creature type, and Starfield of Nyx's "each other non-Aura enchantment you control is a creature in addition to its other types" (Alan controls five enchantments: Iroas, God of Victory, three others, and Starfield of Nyx itself). Neither depends on the other under the 613.8a test, so they apply in timestamp order (613.1, 613.6). Starfield of Nyx's effect has the later timestamp, so it applies last and Iroas, God of Victory ends up a Legendary Enchantment Creature — God.

3. Layer 7b (base P/T). Starfield of Nyx sets base power and base toughness each equal to mana value. Iroas, God of Victory's mana value is 4, so it's 4/4, not its printed 7/4 (613.1g, 613.4a, 302.4c). This setting effect applies in layer 7b regardless of what happened in layer 4 (613.6), and would apply even if the permanent weren't a creature at the time (208.3a).

Timing assumption: I'm treating the question as asking about the state immediately after Starfield of Nyx resolves, with Starfield of Nyx's timestamp later than Iroas, God of Victory's. That's necessarily the case here since Iroas, God of Victory was already on the battlefield. If Alan later stops controlling five enchantments, Starfield of Nyx's effect switches off and Iroas, God of Victory reverts to a non-creature 7/4 enchantment; if devotion to red and white ever reaches seven, it would be a creature either way (7/4 base, still overwritten to 4/4 by Starfield of Nyx while that's active).

Player count doesn't matter here — devotion counts only permanents Alan controls, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Iroas, God of Victory is a creature with power and toughness equal to its mana value.

In the type layer, there are 2 effects that impact Iroas, God of Victory's type. They are applied in timestamp order, so first Iroas, God of Victory's effect causes Iroas, God of Victory to not be a creature, then Starfield of Nyx's ability causes Iroas, God of Victory to become a creature.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Painter's Servant] naming "blue" and [Sword of Body and Mind]. Nico casts [Gift of Tusks] targeting the Painter's Servant. After it resolves, what happens if Autumn tries to equip Painter's Servant with Sword of Body and Mind?

entries.answer:
The equip works: Sword of Body and Mind attaches to Painter's Servant and stays attached.

Why: Equip {2} means "Attach this permanent to target creature you control. Activate only as a sorcery" [702.6a]. Painter's Servant is still a creature (Gift of Tusks makes it a green Elephant with base power and toughness 3/3), it's controlled by Autumn, and an Equipment can legally be attached to a creature [301.5c], so the ability has a legal target and resolves.

The key point is what Gift of Tusks did. Gift of Tusks makes Painter's Servant lose all abilities, so its color-changing ability ("All cards that aren't on the battlefield, spells, and permanents are the chosen color in addition to their other colors") is gone [113.10]. Sword of Body and Mind is therefore just a colorless artifact again, not blue. Sword of Body and Mind grants the equipped creature protection from green and from blue, and protection would force an Equipment with the named quality to become unattached as a state-based action [702.16d, 704.1] — but Sword of Body and Mind is neither green nor blue, so nothing unattaches. (Protection also doesn't care that Painter's Servant itself is green; the quality is checked against the Equipment.) Painter's Servant ends up a 5/5 green Elephant with protection from green and from blue.

Contrast: if Painter's Servant still had its ability naming blue, Sword of Body and Mind would be blue, and the moment it became attached the protection-from-blue it grants would immediately unattach it as a state-based action, leaving it on the battlefield unattached [702.16d, 704.1, 301.5c]. Note also that if some other effect gives Painter's Servant an ability after Gift of Tusks has resolved, it keeps that ability [Gift of Tusks ruling #0], but the original color-changing ability is not coming back this turn.

Timing assumption: Gift of Tusks has already fully resolved before the equip ability is activated, as stated. If instead Gift of Tusks were cast and resolved after Sword of Body and Mind was already attached, the result is the same end state — Sword of Body and Mind stops being blue and remains attached. Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

entries.question: Nathanael controls [Grizzly Bears] and [Muraganda Petroglyphs]. They cast and resolve [Crowd's Favor], targeting Grizzly Bears. Amia then casts [Archetype of Courage]. After it resolves, what are the power and toughness of Grizzly Bears?

entries.answer:
Grizzly Bears ends up 5/4.

Why: characteristics are worked out in the CR 613 layer system (613.1, 613.1g), and abilities are settled in layer 6 before power/toughness in layer 7.

Layer 6 (abilities), in timestamp order (613.7):
- Crowd's Favor granted Grizzly Bears first strike.
- Archetype of Courage, cast later by Amia, says creatures your opponents control "lose first strike and can't have or gain first strike." With the later timestamp, it strips that granted ability. Per 113.12, a granted ability like this can be removed by another effect. So after Archetype of Courage resolves, Grizzly Bears has no abilities at all.

Layer 7c (modify power/toughness, 613.4c, 302.4c):
- Muraganda Petroglyphs ("Creatures with no abilities get +2/+2") now applies again, because Grizzly Bears has no abilities: 2/2 → 4/4.
- Crowd's Favor's +1/+0 still applies — that part of the effect is independent of the first strike grant and is not removed: 4/4 → 5/4.

So the Petroglyphs bonus "turns back on" the instant first strike is stripped; 613.5 confirms these recalculations are continuous and instantaneous.

Timing note: this assumes Crowd's Favor fully resolved before Archetype of Courage was cast, as stated. If instead Archetype of Courage were already on the battlefield when Crowd's Favor resolved, Grizzly Bears still couldn't gain first strike ("can't have or gain"), so it would still be 5/4.

Player count doesn't matter here: Archetype of Courage affects creatures each of its controller's opponents controls, so in a multiplayer game it strips first strike from Grizzly Bears and from every other opponent's creatures identically.

entries.answer_gold: 5/4. In layer 6, Archetype of Courage makes Crowd's Favor unable to grant first strike to Grizzly Bears. entries.question: Abel attacks with [Pristine Angel]. While it's tapped, Nico activates [Cephalid Snitch]'s ability targeting Pristine Angel. After that resolves, Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel. Can Nico now target the Pristine Angel with [Murder]?

Why: Pristine Angel's own text gives it protection from artifacts and from each color only "as long as this creature is untapped." While Pristine Angel was tapped it had no protection at all, but Cephalid Snitch's ability still resolved and applied its continuous effect: Pristine Angel loses protection from black until end of turn. That effect isn't a one-shot "strip what's there now" — it's a continuous effect lasting until end of turn, applied along with all other continuous effects each time the game recalculates Pristine Angel's characteristics (see rules 613.11 and 608.2c on following the instruction as written). So when Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel, Pristine Angel regains protection from artifacts and from each other color, but the Cephalid Snitch effect keeps removing protection from black for the rest of the turn.

Because Pristine Angel has no protection from black, it's a legal target for Murder (a black instant), and it remains a legal target on resolution (608.2b), so it is destroyed. Note also that untapping Pristine Angel after it was declared as an attacker doesn't remove it from combat, and neither does tapping it (506.4b) — that's irrelevant to legality here, just to combat.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Cephalid Snitch's ability fully resolved before Pristine Angel untapped, as stated. If instead Pristine Angel had already untapped before Cephalid Snitch's ability was activated, Pristine Angel would have protection from blue at that moment; whether Cephalid Snitch's ability (from a blue source Nico controls) could target it would then depend on protection from blue, and Nico could not target it. Either way, once the Cephalid Snitch effect is in place, Murder works.

Multiplayer: this works the same with two players or more; nothing here depends on player count. Nico targeting Abel's Pristine Angel does count as committing a crime (700.13, Crime), which matters only if some other card cares about crimes.

entries.answer_gold:
Yes. "Protection from all colors" is shorthand for protection from each color individually. It loses protection from black, and still has protection from all the other colors.

entries.question: Alijah controls [Badlands] and [Conversion]. Alijah then casts [Magus of the Moon]. After that resolves, what color(s) of mana can Badlands tap for?

entries.answer:
Badlands taps for white mana only ({W}). It is a Plains.

Why: both Conversion ("All Mountains are Plains") and Magus of the Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") are continuous type-changing effects applied in layer 4 (subtype-changing). Normally Conversion, with the earlier timestamp, would apply first. But there's a dependency: applying Magus of the Moon changes what Conversion applies to (Badlands, a nonbasic land, becomes a Mountain), so Conversion is applied after Magus of the Moon.

Step by step:
1. Magus of the Moon: Badlands is nonbasic, so its subtypes are set to just Mountain. Per CR 305.7 it loses its old land types (Swamp and Mountain from its printed type line) and the abilities generated from them, and gains "{T}: Add {R}" (Magus of the Moon ruling #4).
2. Conversion: Badlands is now a Mountain, so Conversion sets its type to Plains. Again per CR 305.7 it loses the Mountain type and the red mana ability, and gains "{T}: Add {W}" (CR 305.6 — any land with the Plains subtype has "{T}: Add {W}").

So Badlands ends up as a nonbasic land with the single land type Plains and exactly one mana ability: {T}: Add {W}. No black, no red. Note Magus of the Moon doesn't change names or supertypes (Magus of the Moon ruling #1), and Conversion doesn't touch the snow supertype (Conversion ruling #1) — Badlands is still named Badlands and is still nonbasic.

Also note there's no window to tap Badlands for {R} "in between": continuous effects apply immediately and simultaneously in the layer system, they don't resolve one at a time (Conversion ruling #0).

If Conversion is sacrificed (it's sacrificed at your upkeep unless you pay {W}{W}), Badlands reverts to being just a Mountain from Magus of the Moon and taps for {R}. If Magus of the Moon leaves, Conversion once more applies directly to the printed Mountain type and Badlands is still a Plains tapping for {W}.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players — both cards affect permanents regardless of controller, and Alijah controls all three here.

entries.answer_gold: Only {R}. Both Magus of the Moon and Conversion only apply in layer 4. The effects are applied in timestamp order, resulting in Conversion applying first to make Badlands a Plains, then Magus of the Moon applies making it a Mountain.

entries.question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?

entries.question: Ariah controls [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nickolas casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics after Turn to Frog resolves?
entries.reason: Both conclude Wayward Angel ends up a 4/4 blue Frog with no abilities because its +3/+3 from the threshold began applying before Turn to Frog removed its abilities.
entries.answer:
Wayward Angel becomes a 4/4 blue Frog creature with no abilities (still named Wayward Angel, controlled by Ariah), for the rest of the turn.

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.1g, 613.7):
- Layer 4 (types): Turn to Frog makes it a Frog — it loses Angel and Horror, remaining a Creature — Frog.
- Layer 5 (color): the threshold ability (earlier timestamp) makes it black — and only black, not white and black (Wayward Angel ruling #0) — then Turn to Frog (later timestamp) makes it blue. Net: blue only.
- Layer 6 (abilities): the threshold ability applies first (granting trample and the upkeep sacrifice trigger), then Turn to Frog removes all abilities, including flying, vigilance, the threshold ability itself, and everything it granted. Net: no abilities.
- Layer 7b: Turn to Frog sets base power and toughness to 1/1 (CR 613.4b; Turn to Frog ruling #0 — it overwrites earlier setting effects).
- Layer 7c: here's the catch — because the threshold ability already began applying in layer 5 before it was removed in layer 6, its +3/+3 still applies in layer 7c (CR 613.6 as reflected in the layer ordering; compare Turn to Frog ruling #4, where a God's type-changing ability applies even though the same spell removes it). So 1/1 + 3/+3 = 4/4.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Ariah has seven or more cards in the graveyard both when Turn to Frog resolves and while you're checking characteristics. If the graveyard drops below seven afterward, the threshold ability is no longer generating any effect (and it's been removed anyway), so Wayward Angel would just be a 1/1 blue Frog with no abilities.

Nothing here depends on the player count: the same result holds in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since only Wayward Angel is affected and control doesn't change.

entries.answer_gold: It's a 4/4 blue Frog with no abilities. Wayward Angel's last ability begins to apply in layer 5. It's removed by Turn to Frog in layer 6, but since it's already started to apply, it will continue doing so in later layers. Wayward Angel has the earlier timestamp, so it gives itself trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature" before Turn to Frog removes its abilities in layer 6.

entries.question: Ariella controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathaniel casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?

2. Turning it face up doesn't remove Turn to Frog's effect: as a face-down permanent is turned face up its copiable values revert to Wayward Angel's normal printed values, but any effects already applied to it still apply ([708.8], [708.10]). So now Turn to Frog's effect is applied on top of a real 4/4 white Angel Horror with flying, vigilance, and threshold, with 7 cards in Ariella's graveyard.

3. Layering ([613.1], [613.1g], [613.7]) — Turn to Frog has the earlier timestamp; the threshold ability only becomes an ability of the object when it's turned face up, so its effect has the later timestamp:
   - Layer 4 (types): Turn to Frog makes it a Frog, wiping Angel Horror. It keeps the Creature card type ([Turn to Frog ruling #1]).
   - Layer 5 (color): Turn to Frog makes it blue, then threshold (later timestamp) makes it black — and black only, not white-and-black ([Wayward Angel ruling #0]).
   - Layer 6 (abilities): Turn to Frog removes all abilities (killing flying, vigilance, and the threshold ability itself). But because the threshold effect had already started applying in layer 5, CR 613.6 says it continues to apply in every later layer even though the ability generating it is gone — so it still grants trample and the upkeep sacrifice trigger at its later timestamp.    - Layer 7b: Turn to Frog sets base P/T to 1/1 ([Turn to Frog ruling #0]); layer 7c: threshold's +3/+3 still applies, giving 4/4.

4. Anything Wayward Angel gains after Turn to Frog resolved it keeps ([Turn to Frog ruling #3]). Note also that turning it face up doesn't trigger enters-the-battlefield abilities ([708.8]).

If instead it were turned face up first and Turn to Frog resolved after, Turn to Frog would have the later timestamp: it would then be a 1/1 blue Frog with no abilities at all (threshold's layer-5/6/7 effects all being overwritten or removed by the later effect).

Wayward Angel receives a new timestamp when it turns face up, so its ability is applied before Turn to Frog in each layer. Wayward Angel's last ability is removed by Turn to Frog in layer 6, but since it's already started to apply in layer 5 to change its color to black, it will continue doing so in later layers. Turn to Frog has the earlier timestamp, so it makes Wayward Angel blue before it becomes black in layer 5 and removes Wayward Angel's abilities in layer 6 before it gains trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature".

entries.question: Ahmad controls [Conspiracy] (naming "Ferret"), [Kormus Bell], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth], and a [Vastwood Zendikon] enchanting Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature? If so, what are its creature types?

4. Conspiracy makes creatures Ahmad controls the chosen type, Ferret, and they lose all their other creature types [Conspiracy ruling #4], [Conspiracy ruling #1]. At this point Conspiracy is no longer be dependent on Vastwood Zendikon, so Conspiracy is applied, and then Vastwood Zendikon. Winged Temple of Orazca is a nonbasic (Legendary) land, so Blood Moon sets its subtype to Mountain and, per Blood Moon ruling #2, strips its other land types and its printed abilities, giving it "{T}: Add {R}." 1. If Prismatic Omen's type-setting applies after Blood Moon's: subtypes are Mountain, Plains, Island, Swamp, Forest → taps for {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G} (one mana of your choice among those).
2. If Blood Moon's applies after Prismatic Omen's: subtypes are just Mountain → taps for {R} only.

Either way the printed "any color" ability and the {1}{G}{U}, {T} ability are gone, and note {C} is never available here — colorless is not a color ([105.1], [105.4], [Colorless]).

Multiplayer note: nothing changes with more than two players; these are Adan's own permanents and no rule provided here makes the outcome depend on the number of opponents.

What's missing from the provided context: the timestamp/tiebreak rule (CR 613.7 family) for permanents entering the battlefield simultaneously. If a later-applied Prismatic Omen is chosen, you get all five colors; otherwise just red.

entries.question: Apollo controls [Realmwright] naming "Island", [Arcane Adaptation] naming "Saproling", and [Life and Limb], which entered the battlefield in that order. What are the types and subtypes of Realmwright?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Realmwright also becomes an Island (gaining Island from its own ability applied after Life and Limb), but the reference says Realmwright's effect applies earlier and thus it does not gain Island, so the final type lists differ.
entries.answer:
Realmwright ends up as a **Land Creature — Vedalken Wizard Saproling Forest Island**, and it's a green 1/1.

How it gets there (all in layer 4 for types/subtypes):

1. **Arcane Adaptation** (naming Saproling) makes every creature Apollo controls that type in addition to its others, so Realmwright becomes a Vedalken Wizard Saproling. Saproling is a legal creature type to name (Arcane Adaptation ruling #1, CR 205.3m).
2. **Life and Limb** then sees Realmwright as a Saproling, so it applies: Realmwright becomes a 1/1 green Saproling creature and Forest land in addition to its other types. It keeps the creature type and gains the land card type, plus subtypes Saproling and Forest. Per CR 205.1b, "in addition to their other types" means all prior card types and subtypes are retained. Per Life and Limb ruling #3, each subtype stays correlated to the right card type: Forest is a land type only, Saproling is a creature type only (CR 205.3c, 205.3i, 205.3m).
3. **Realmwright's own** static ability ("Lands you control are the chosen type in addition to their other types," naming Island) now applies to Realmwright itself, because Life and Limb made it a land. Even though Realmwright has the earliest timestamp, its effect is applied *after* Life and Limb's: applying Life and Limb changes what Realmwright's effect applies to, so Realmwright's effect is dependent on it (dependency, not timestamp, sets the order). Realmwright therefore also gains the land type Island. Island is a basic land type, a legal choice (Realmwright ruling #1, CR 305.6).

Consequences: as a land with the basic land types Forest and Island, Realmwright has the intrinsic mana abilities "{T}: Add {G}" and "{T}: Add {U}" (CR 305.6) — though as a creature it's subject to summoning sickness for tapping. In layer 5 Life and Limb sets its color to green (it is no longer blue), and in layer 7b its power and toughness are set to 1/1. It has no supertypes, and none are added or removed (CR 205.4b).

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same at a two-player or multiplayer table, since all three permanents only affect permanents Apollo controls or all Forests/Saprolings.

entries.answer_gold:
Realmwright is a 1/1 green Land Creature - Vedalken Wizard Saproling Forest.

All three cards have effects in layer 4, the type changing layer. The game first looks at Realmwright's effect since it's first in timestamp order, sees that it's not dependent on Arcane Adaptation nor on Life and Limb, and applies it. Next the game looks at Arcane Adaptation's effect, sees that it's not dependent on Life and Limb, and applies it, followed by Life and Limb last.

entries.question: Ainsley controls [Leyline of Singularity] and [Awoken Demon] equipped with [Helm of the Host]. When the trigger from Helm of the Host resolves, will the created token be legendary?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the Helm-created token is made legendary by Leyline of Singularity despite Helm's "isn't legendary" clause, so the legend rule will force the controller to choose one.
entries.answer:
Yes — the token will be legendary once it's on the battlefield, and the legend rule will then force Ainsley to keep only one of the two Awoken Demons.

Why: Helm of the Host's copy effect says the token "isn't legendary," so as a copiable value the token starts out non-legendary (Helm of the Host ruling #3). But Leyline of Singularity is a separate continuous static effect that says "All nonland permanents are legendary," and it applies to the token as soon as the token is on the battlefield, independent of copy effects. Adding the legendary supertype doesn't remove the token's other supertypes or change its types (Leyline of Singularity ruling #0, [205.4b]).

Consequence: the token is a copy of Awoken Demon, so it has the name Awoken Demon, the same as the original creature Ainsley controls. Because Leyline of Singularity makes both the token and the original Awoken Demon legendary, and both are controlled by Ainsley with the same name, the legend rule state-based action applies: Ainsley chooses one to keep and the other is put into its owner's graveyard ([704.5j], [205.4d]). Leyline of Singularity ruling #2 confirms this outcome specifically for tokens. If Ainsley keeps the token, it has haste from Helm of the Host; if Ainsley keeps the original Awoken Demon, the token goes to the graveyard and then ceases to exist. Either way Helm of the Host stays attached to whichever creature it was equipped to (it doesn't attach to the token).

Note that with Leyline of Singularity out, Helm of the Host's "isn't legendary" exception is effectively neutralized — the exception normally exists precisely to dodge the legend rule (Helm of the Host ruling #3), but Leyline of Singularity re-applies the supertype afterward.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; Leyline of Singularity and the legend rule both apply per-player, so the result is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. When Helm of the Host goes to create the token of Awoken Demon it will see that it is legendary, and create a token that does not have the legendary supertype. However Leyline of Singularity is generating a continuous effect in layer 4, which will overwrite the base characteristics of any object on the battlefield, regardless of when it entered, making it legendary.

entries.question: Addison controls [Dryad of the Ilysian Grove] and casts [Blood Moon]. What are the characteristics of [Snow-Covered Island], [Study Hall], [Dryad Arbor], and [Mountain] after Blood Moon resolves?

entries.question: Angelina has seven cards in their hand, controls [Trusted Advisor], and casts [Null Profusion]. After Angelina discards at the end of the turn, how many cards should they have in their hand?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Null Profusion sets Angelina's maximum hand size to two, overriding Trusted Advisor's +2, so she discards down to two cards.
entries.answer:
Angelina ends up with two cards in hand.

Because Null Profusion entered the battlefield after Trusted Advisor, its effect is applied later in timestamp order and simply sets Angelina's maximum hand size to two, overwriting the earlier result [Trusted Advisor ruling #0], [Null Profusion ruling #3]. Trusted Advisor's "+2" was applied first (7 + 2 = 9), then Null Profusion's "Your maximum hand size is two" sets the value flatly to 2. Card text like this overrides the normal default of seven [402.2].

Maximum hand size is the number a player must discard down to during their cleanup step: immediately after the cleanup step begins, if the active player's hand has more cards than their maximum hand size, they discard enough cards to reduce it to that number, as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [514.1], [703.4n], [Maximum Hand Size].

Timing note: I'm assuming Null Profusion resolved and was on the battlefield before Angelina's cleanup step, and that the seven cards counted included Null Profusion itself (so six remain after casting it) — either way the discard brings the hand to two. If Null Profusion somehow were not on the battlefield at cleanup (countered, destroyed, etc.), only Trusted Advisor would apply and Angelina's maximum hand size would be nine, so no discard would happen. Also note this discard only occurs during Angelina's own cleanup step, i.e., on Angelina's turn.

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

entries.answer_gold: Two. Trusted Advisor adds two to the maximum hand size (making it nine), and Null Profusion then sets the maximum hand to two.

entries.question: Nico controls [Thespian's Stage] that's currently a copy of [Temple of Triumph]. Alayna casts [Alpine Moon] and names "Temple of Triumph" as it resolves. Alayna then activates a second Thespian's Stage targeting Temple of Triumph. What does each Thespian's Stage look like?

entries.answer:
Nico's Thespian's Stage is a land named Temple of Triumph with no land types and only one ability: "{T}: Add one mana of any color." Alayna's Thespian's Stage becomes a full, unmolested copy of Temple of Triumph that also keeps a Thespian's Stage copy ability.

Its name is therefore Temple of Triumph, so Alpine Moon's static effect applies to it (Nico is Alayna's opponent): in layer 4 it loses all land types (Temple of Triumph has none printed anyway) and in layer 6 it loses all abilities -- including the granted Thespian's Stage copy ability and the enters-tapped/scry/mana abilities -- then gains "{T}: Add one mana of any color" from that same Alpine Moon effect (CR 613.6, 613.7, 613.8). When Alayna's Stage copies Nico's Stage (the permanent named Temple of Triumph), it copies copiable values only -- Alpine Moon's ability-removal is a layer 6 effect, not copiable, so it isn't copied (CR 707.2). So Alayna's Stage is a land named Temple of Triumph with "This land enters tapped," "When this land enters, scry 1," "{T}: Add {R} or {W}," and the Thespian's Stage copy ability (present from Nico's copy exception and re-added by Alayna's own "except it has this ability"; duplicates are redundant, CR 707.9a). The enters-tapped and scry abilities do nothing now, since it was already on the battlefield (Thespian's Stage ruling #1), and it doesn't untap (ruling #2).

Assumption: Alayna's activation targeted Nico's Stage (the only permanent named Temple of Triumph). If she instead targeted some genuine Temple of Triumph land she or someone else controls, the result for her Stage is identical.

Multiplayer: nothing changes structurally -- Alpine Moon hits the named lands controlled by *each* of Alpine Moon's controller's opponents, so in a bigger game every opponent's Temple of Triumph-named land is stripped the same way, while Alayna's own stays intact.

entries.answer_gold: Both Thespian's Stages are lands named "Temple of Triumph" and have "{T}: Add one mana of any color." and no other abilities. entries.question: Allen controls [Thraben Purebloods] which is enchanted by [Kenrith's Transformation]. Thraben Purebloods then becomes enchanted by [One with the Stars]. What happens?

entries.answer:

Because the Elk creature type is a subtype tied to the creature card type it just lost, Thraben Purebloods loses the Elk subtype too (One with the Stars ruling #2). Any supertypes would be kept.
- Thraben Purebloods is still green, and the 3/3 base power/toughness setting effect from Kenrith's Transformation still technically applies, but power and toughness are meaningless while it isn't a creature. One caveat: Kenrith's Transformation says "Enchant creature," and Thraben Purebloods is no longer a creature, so Kenrith's Transformation is no longer legally attached (rule 702.5c requires the enchanted object to match all enchant abilities). The provided rules don't include the state-based action that handles an Aura attached to an illegal object, so I can't cite what happens to it from this context. If Kenrith's Transformation does leave the battlefield, its effects end and Thraben Purebloods reverts to being a white Dog with its own printed characteristics — but One with the Stars keeps it an enchantment and not a creature (One with the Stars ruling #1 shows that effect persists even when the creature-ness came from elsewhere).

This is an interaction of continuous effects, so the layers will need to be considered. In this case, no changes occur until layer four. There are two effects occurring in this layer, so timestamps will need to be considered. Since Kenrith's Transformation was attached first, Thraben Purebloods maintains its status as a creature. Then, One with the Stars turns Thraben Purebloods into an enchantment and removes all other types. Thraben Purebloods is changed to the color dictated by Kenrith's Transformation in layer five. entries.question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
entries.reason: The candidate asserts Trumpeting Gnarr's mutate-triggered ability remains and triggers on the merge, creating a 3/3 token, whereas the reference states the resulting permanent is a face-down 2/2 with no abilities and that Gnarr's ability does not trigger.
entries.answer:
The resulting mutated permanent is a face-down 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no card types other than creature, no mana cost, and no subtypes — because a merged permanent takes its other characteristics from its topmost component, and here the topmost component is the face-down manifested card ([730.2a], [702.140e]). As it resolved it did not enter the battlefield; it merged with the manifested creature, and Avery chose to put it underneath ([702.140c], [608.3d], [730.2a]). Practical notes: the permanent is still face down and still has "phased in / face down" status ([110.5]), so Avery may later turn it face up for its mana cost if the manifested card is a creature card (per Soul Summons); if it's turned face up, that face-up card's characteristics become the topmost component's characteristics, while the Trumpeting Gnarr ability underneath is retained. Had Avery instead put Trumpeting Gnarr on top, the permanent would be a 3/3 green Beast named Trumpeting Gnarr with that same mutate trigger. Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

entries.question: April casts [Spontaneous Flight] targeting their [Mist Dragon]. After that resolves April then activates its 'lose flying' ability. They cast another Spontaneous Flight targeting Mist Dragon. After that resolves they then use [Hex Parasite] to remove one flying counter. Does Mist Dragon have flying?
entries.reason: Both conclude Mist Dragon still has flying because layer-6 effects are applied by timestamp, the second flying counter is newer than the lose-flying activation, and Hex Parasite leaves one newer flying counter.
entries.answer:
Yes — Mist Dragon still has flying, and it's an 8/8.

Why: everything here is sorted in layer 6 (ability adding/removing, including keyword counters) by timestamp (CR 613.1, 613.1f, 613.7a). In order:
1. Spontaneous Flight #1 puts a flying counter on Mist Dragon — Mist Dragon has flying (and +2/+2 in layer 7c).
2. April activates Mist Dragon's "{0}: This creature loses flying" — that removal has a later timestamp, so it beats the first counter and Mist Dragon has no flying (CR 113.10b, 113.10c, 613.9). Note the removal effect lasts indefinitely; it does not remove the counter itself, it just out-timestamps it.
3. Spontaneous Flight #2 puts a second flying counter on Mist Dragon, with the latest timestamp of all three effects. Most recent wins, so Mist Dragon has flying again (and is now 8/8 from the two +2/+2 effects).
4. Hex Parasite removes one flying counter. One flying counter remains. Since the two flying counters are identical objects on the permanent and the surviving one is treated as the still-existing later counter, its timestamp is still later than the "loses flying" activation, so Mist Dragon keeps flying.

Assumption on the ambiguous point: which of the two indistinguishable flying counters Hex Parasite "removed." Counters of the same kind aren't tracked separately, so the remaining flying counter is just "a flying counter now on Mist Dragon," post-dating the lose-flying effect. If instead you insisted the surviving counter were the pre-lose-flying one, the "{0}: loses flying" effect would be the latest layer-6 effect and Mist Dragon would not have flying — but there's no rules basis for distinguishing the counters that way. Also note Hex Parasite only gets +1/+0 for counters actually removed (Hex Parasite ruling #0), so it gets +1/+0 here.

If April wants Mist Dragon to lose flying, she can simply activate "{0}: This creature loses flying" again for a fresh, latest timestamp. Nothing here depends on the number of players; it's a one-sided sequence of April's own actions, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games (in multiplayer, other players holding removal-of-flying effects could of course respond, and per CR 732.3 the player acting last in such a back-and-forth determines the final state).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Keyword counters and ability-removing effects all apply in layer 6 in timestamp order. However when April put the second flying counter on Mist Dragon all flying counters on Mist Dragon had their timestamps updated to match the most recent counter. Meaning that the remaining flying counter on Mist Dragon has a newer timestamp than the activation of the ability that causes it to lose flying.

entries.question: Avery casts [Vulpikeet] for its mutate cost, mutating under a 1/1 red Goblin creature token. They then cast [Rootborn Defenses], choosing to populate the merged permanent. What happens?

entries.answer:
Avery can populate the merged permanent, because its topmost component is the Goblin creature token, so the merged permanent is a creature token Avery controls. The new token is a copy of that merged permanent's copiable characteristics — a 1/1 red Goblin with flying and "Whenever this creature mutates, put a +1/+1 counter on it" — and it, along with Avery's other creatures at that moment, gains indestructible until end of turn.

Details:

- Mutate: casting Vulpikeet for its mutate cost makes it a mutating creature spell targeting a non-Human creature Avery owns [702.140a]. On resolution Vulpikeet doesn't enter the battlefield separately; it merges with the Goblin token into one object represented by more than one card/token, and Avery chose to put Vulpikeet on the bottom [702.140c, 730.1, 608.3d]. The mutated permanent has all abilities of both components (so it has flying and Vulpikeet's mutate trigger), but all its other characteristics — name, types, colors, power/toughness — come from the topmost component, the 1/1 red Goblin token [702.140e]. Vulpikeet's own "whenever this creature mutates" ability triggered and put a +1/+1 counter on it [702.140d], making it 2/2 on the battlefield.

- What the copy looks like: characteristic changes from merging an object with a permanent are copiable effects applied in layer 1a [613.2a], so the copy takes the merged permanent's copiable values: a 1/1 red Goblin creature token with flying and the mutate-triggered ability. It is a single new token, not a merged pile — Vulpikeet itself stays where it is, under the original. Non-copiable things like the +1/+1 counter and any temporary pumps aren't copied, so the new token is 1/1.
- Indestructible: Rootborn Defenses grants indestructible until end of turn to the creatures Avery controls after populating, including the freshly created token, but not to creatures Avery comes to control later in the turn [Rootborn Defenses ruling #0]. That includes the merged permanent itself.

Nothing here depends on player count; the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since populate and Rootborn Defenses only involve Avery's own creatures.

entries.answer_gold: They will create a token that is a copy of the 1/1 red Goblin creature token with all abilities from Vulpikeet. To populate means to create a copy of a creature token the player controls. A mutated permanent has the characteristics of its topmost component, along with all abilities of each card and token that represents it, so it will be a token and can therefore be populated. ([702.140e], [729.2d]) This is a copyable effect, so the copy created when Avery populates the merged permanent will also have the characteristics of the Goblin token and the abilities from Vulpikeet.

entries.question: Aimee controls [Fiend Artisan] and has four creature cards in their graveyard. Nico enchants it with [Mystic Subdual]. What is the power and toughness of Fiend Artisan?

Why: Fiend Artisan is printed 1/1, and its "gets +1/+1 for each creature card in your graveyard" is an ordinary static ability that would apply in layer 7c ([613.4c]), not a characteristic-defining ability that sets power/toughness (compare [604.3], [208.2a] — Fiend Artisan's printed box is 1/1, not */*). Note the contrast drawn by [Mystic Subdual ruling #1]: that ruling covers creatures printed */* whose power/toughness comes from a characteristic-defining ability — those become 0/0 base and then -2/0. entries.question: Ari controls [Xathrid Gorgon]. Neriah controls a [Hexavus] and [Stonehewer Giant]. Ari activates Xathrid Gorgon to put a petrification counter on Stonehewer Giant which Neriah removes with Hexavus. Can Neriah activate Stonehewer Giant's activated ability?

Multiplayer: this doesn't change with more than two players — Humility says "all creatures," regardless of controller.

entries.question: Alex controls [Magus of the Moon] and [Forgotten Monument]. Neil casts [Lizard, Connors's Curse] targeting Magus of the Moon. After Lizard, Connors's Curse has resolved, what are the characteristics of Forgotten Monument?

entries.question: Ainsley enchants their [Colossus Hammer] with [Rune of Flight]. Then they equip it to [Skeletal Snake]. Does Skeletal Snake have flying?

That granted ability's timestamp is Rune of Flight's timestamp, since that's later than Colossus Hammer's own timestamp [613.7a]. Colossus Hammer's printed ability "Equipped creature gets +10/+10 and loses flying" has the earlier timestamp of the two.

When Colossus Hammer becomes attached to Skeletal Snake, Colossus Hammer receives a new timestamp [613.7e], and both of its abilities (its own and the one granted by Rune of Flight) receive new timestamps — but their relative order is preserved [613.7a]. Adding and removing abilities is not governed by the "can't beats can" rule, so "loses flying" doesn't automatically trump [101.2a, 113.10].

Separately, in layer 7c, Colossus Hammer's +10/+10 still applies, making Skeletal Snake 12/11.

Order matters here: this is the case where Rune of Flight was attached to Colossus Hammer *before* Colossus Hammer was equipped, as stated. If instead Colossus Hammer were already equipped to Skeletal Snake and Rune of Flight came down afterward, the answer is the same — Rune of Flight's granted ability is still later, and Colossus Hammer's own ruling confirms that a creature gaining flying after Colossus Hammer is attached keeps flying [Colossus Hammer ruling #2]. entries.question: Ari controls [Magus of the Moon] enchanted with [Ichthyomorphosis]. Is Ari's [Dormant Volcano] a Mountain?

entries.question: Averie controls [Muraganda Petroglyphs] and [Wayward Angel], and has more than 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathan casts and resolves [Humility]. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics?

Player count doesn't change anything here; the provided rules and cards involve no defending-player or per-opponent choices, so the answer is identical in two-player and multiplayer games ("your graveyard" is Averie's graveyard either way).

Applying layers in order:
- In layer 5, Wayward Angel becomes black. 
- In layer 6 there are two contending effects: Wayward Angel's ability giving it trample and an upkeep triggered ability, and Humility's ability removing all abilities from Wayward Angel. There is no dependency between the two, since Wayward Angel's ability has already started applying in a previous layer, and will continue to apply even if removed by Humility's ability. entries.question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: Jinx removes Urza's Saga's chapter abilities (while it remains a Saga), causing it to be immediately sacrificed as a state-based action.
entries.answer:
Alexzander's Jinx makes Nico's Urza's Saga lose its chapter abilities, and since it's still a Saga, Nico must immediately sacrifice it as a state-based action.

Details:

1. Jinx says "Target land becomes the basic land type of your choice until end of turn," so Alexzander chooses a basic land type for Urza's Saga. Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type makes the land lose its old land type (Urza's Saga) and lose all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and copiable effects affecting it; it gains the mana ability of the chosen basic land type [305.7]. The chapter abilities (I, II, III) are printed rules-text abilities, so they're gone.

2. Land types are land subtypes; Saga is an *enchantment* subtype, and setting a land's subtype only replaces subtypes from that set (land types) [201.1a-style rule 205.1a]. So Urza's Saga is still an enchantment Saga — with no chapter abilities and two lore counters on it.

3. That situation is exactly the one covered by the Urza's Saga ruling: "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed" [Urza's Saga ruling #1]. This sacrifice happens as a state-based action the next time a player would receive priority; it doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to [704.5s, 714.4].

4. Abilities Urza's Saga already *gained* from chapters I and II ({T}: Add {C}, and the {2}, {T} Construct-token ability) were granted by resolved effects rather than by its own rules text, so rule 305.7 doesn't strip those [305.7, Urza's Saga ruling #5] — but that hardly matters, since Nico sacrifices the permanent right away. If Nico wants value, he should activate the Construct-token ability (if he has {2} and it's untapped) before priority passes back — practically, Alexzander casting Jinx puts the ability on the stack and Nico can respond while Jinx is still on the stack, before the type change happens.

Assumed timing: I'm reading this as Jinx resolving while Urza's Saga has two lore counters and no chapter ability of its own on the stack. If instead a chapter ability of Urza's Saga were still on the stack, the sacrifice would be delayed only in the case covered by [714.4]/[704.5s] (a Saga isn't sacrificed while it's the source of a triggered chapter ability that hasn't left the stack) — but with the chapter abilities removed, the ruling's immediate sacrifice still applies once that ability finishes resolving.

Player count: nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games, since Jinx targets a single land and the sacrifice is performed by that land's controller, Nico.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
In layer 4, Urza's Saga will have its land type overwritten as well as lose all of its chapter abilities. It will gain the abilities to tap for {C} and to create Construct tokens in layer 6, as those abilities are granted by a continuous effect that was generated when the previous chapter abilities resolved..

Because Urza's Saga has lost all of its chapter abilities while still being a Saga, it is immediately sacrificed the next time state-based actions are checked, per the Urza's Saga ruling "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed".

entries.question: Aaden activates [Inkmoth Nexus], equips [Colossus Hammer] to it, then activates Inkmoth Nexus again. What are the characteristics of Inkmoth Nexus?

Inkmoth Nexus ends up as an 11/11 colorless Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature land with flying and infect (plus its own two activated abilities).

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.7, timestamp order within each layer):
- Layer 4 (types): both activations of Inkmoth Nexus make it an artifact creature — Phyrexian Blinkmoth — and it's still a land. Applying the same effect twice changes nothing further.
- Layer 6 (abilities): first activation (timestamp 1) grants flying and infect; Colossus Hammer (timestamp 2 — an Equipment gets a new timestamp when it becomes attached, CR 613.7e) removes flying; the second activation of Inkmoth Nexus (timestamp 3) grants flying and infect again. Because that grant has the latest timestamp in layer 6, Inkmoth Nexus has flying. Colossus Hammer's "loses flying" only strips flying that exists when it's applied; it doesn't stop a later effect from granting it back.
- Layer 7b (setting P/T): both Inkmoth Nexus activations set it to 1/1; the later one wins, still 1/1.
- Layer 7c (modifications): Colossus Hammer's +10/+10 applies after, giving 11/11.

So the order matters: had Aaden equipped Colossus Hammer after the second activation, Colossus Hammer's ability would have the latest timestamp in layer 6 and Inkmoth Nexus would lose flying (it would still be 11/11 with infect).

Colors: nothing here changes color, so Inkmoth Nexus remains colorless (becoming an artifact doesn't grant a color). Timing assumption: all three actions resolved in the order stated, all during the same turn, so both animation effects are still active ("until end of turn").

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's identical in two-player and multiplayer games. Note also Inkmoth Nexus ruling #0/#1: it can only attack or tap for mana if Aaden has controlled it continuously since his most recent turn began.

entries.answer_gold: It's an 11/11 with infect and flying. The gaining and losing flying effects are applied in timestamp order. Since the most recent one gives Inkmoth Nexus flying, it has flying. entries.question: Alvin controls [Mycosynth Lattice], a [Dance of the Dead] attached to a [Streetbreaker Wurm] that it returned to the battlefield, and a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that is currently a copy of [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] due to its second ability. Alvin casts [Eureka], choosing to put [March of the Machines] onto the battlefield, then putting [Copy Artifact] onto the battlefield, which copies the Mizzium Transreliquat and then copies the Dance of the Dead with its new copy ability. (The one from Sakashima of a Thousand Faces.) They choose for it to enchant a [Viashino Warrior] in their graveyard. As Eureka continues resolving, they put [Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked] onto the battlefield and sacrifice March of the Machines. After Copy Artifact's trigger resolves and returns the Viashino Warrior to the battlefield, Alvin activates the ability of the Copy Artifact to turn it into a copy of Streetbreaker Wurm. What happens?
entries.reason: While both say the Viashino stays and the Copy becomes unattached, the candidate incorrectly states Dance's leave-the-battlefield sacrifice ability is gone (implying no later sacrifice), whereas the reference says the sacrifice trigger can still occur if the copied permanent later leaves.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: the ability resolves, and the Copy Artifact permanent stops being a Dance of the Dead Aura and becomes a 6/4 Wurm named Streetbreaker Wurm, keeping only the {1}{U}{R} copy ability it granted itself. Because it never left the battlefield, Dance of the Dead's "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it" ability is simply gone rather than triggering, so the Viashino Warrior stays on the battlefield as a plain 4/2, no longer enchanted, no longer +1/+1, and no longer barred from untapping.

Why it works:

1. Legal target: Streetbreaker Wurm is a permanent, and Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts in addition to their other types, so Streetbreaker Wurm is a legal target for the "{1}{U}{R}: This artifact becomes a copy of target artifact, except it has this ability" ability that the Copy Artifact permanent inherited (via Mizzium Transreliquat's copiable values, which were Sakashima of a Thousand Faces plus that ability — see Mizzium Transreliquat rulings #0 and #3, and 707.9b).

2. New copy effect overwrites the old one: a permanent that becomes a copy of something else takes on the new copiable values entirely; it doesn't stack the previous copy effect on top (707.3, 707.4, Mizzium Transreliquat rulings #0 and #4). So the Copy Artifact permanent loses Dance of the Dead's text, loses the "it's an enchantment in addition to its other types" modification from Copy Artifact's own entry, and loses Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' abilities. All it retains is Streetbreaker Wurm's copiable values plus the {1}{U}{R} ability, because that ability's own exception re-grants it (707.9b).

3. No leaves-the-battlefield or enters-the-battlefield triggers: becoming a copy of a different object while remaining on the battlefield doesn't cause ETB or LTB abilities to trigger (707.4). The Dance of the Dead sacrifice clause is therefore never triggered — it ceased to exist as an ability while the permanent stayed put — so the returned Viashino Warrior survives.

4. Attachment: since the permanent is no longer an Aura, it can't remain attached to Viashino Warrior; it simply becomes an unattached permanent the next time state-based actions are checked (compare Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3, which unattaches an Aura that becomes a creature).

5. It's an artifact creature: March of the Machines was sacrificed to Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked, so nothing is animating noncreature artifacts, but that's irrelevant here — the permanent is a creature because it copies Streetbreaker Wurm, and it's also an artifact because of Mycosynth Lattice. It entered the battlefield this turn, so it has summoning sickness (it can't attack or use {T} abilities this turn).

6. Alvin's original Dance of the Dead on the real Streetbreaker Wurm is untouched; that Wurm is still enchanted, +1/+1, and doesn't untap normally.

Timing note: as written, the activation is described during Eureka's resolution, which isn't actually possible — I'm assuming Alvin activated the {1}{U}{R} ability after Eureka finished resolving and after the Aura-copy's trigger had already put Viashino Warrior onto the battlefield. If instead the copy ability had resolved before Viashino Warrior was put onto the battlefield, the Dance of the Dead text (and thus the pending trigger's effect) would already be gone from that permanent and Viashino Warrior would never have left the graveyard.

So at end of turn Capenna Express stops being an artifact creature and is left as a permanent that is only an enchantment (a card whose own text is overridden by One with the Stars).

If instead One with the Stars somehow resolved after the crew ability, the outcome is effectively the same for this turn's combat only in reverse: One with the Stars would then strip the artifact and creature types, so Capenna Express couldn't attack or block, and it stays an enchantment thereafter.

Player count doesn't matter here: nothing in this interaction depends on the number of players, and the rules provided contain no multiplayer-specific provisions for it beyond the general note that a replacement effect can't reach outside a player's range of influence (801.13a), which isn't in play.

entries.question:
Alison controls [Mycosynth Lattice], an [Animate Dead] attached to a [Great-Horn Krushok] that it returned to the battlefield, a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that copied [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] with its second ability, and a [Southern Elephant] enchanted by a [Deep Freeze].

Alison casts [Eureka], choosing to put [March of the Machines] onto the battlefield. Alison then puts [Sculpting Steel] onto the battlefield, choosing to copy the Mizzium Transreliquat and then choosing to copy the Animate Dead with its new copy ability. They choose to enchant a [Gigantosaurus] in their graveyard. As Eureka continues resolving, they put [Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked] onto the battlefield and sacrifice March of the Machines.

After Sculpting Steel's trigger resolves and returns the Gigantosaurus to the battlefield, Alison activates the ability of the Sculpting Steel to turn it into a copy of Deep Freeze. After that resolves, they casts [Enchantment Alteration] to attach it to the Southern Elephant. What happens?

entries.answer:

Step by step:

1. **Sculpting Steel's entry.** Sculpting Steel copies Mizzium Transreliquat, which was already a copy of Sakashima of a Thousand Faces via its second ability ("except it has this ability"). Copy effects copy the results of other copy effects, and abilities granted as part of a copying process become part of the copiable values ([707.9a], [707.9b], [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #3], [Sculpting Steel ruling #4]). So Sculpting Steel's copiable values are Sakashima of a Thousand Faces plus "{1}{U}{R}: This artifact becomes a copy of target artifact, except it has this ability."
2. **Sakashima's own replacement effect then applies**, letting Sculpting Steel instead enter as a copy of another creature Alison controls. Animate Dead is a creature at that moment (Mycosynth Lattice makes it an artifact, March of the Machines makes noncreature artifacts creatures). Sculpting Steel enters as Animate Dead, still keeping Sakashima's other abilities and the Transreliquat ability — those are characteristic modifications that stay in the copiable values, not the kind of separate "additional effect" that gets lost under [707.9e]. New "as enters" choices are made by Alison ([707.6]), so it enchants Gigantosaurus in the graveyard and its trigger returns Gigantosaurus to the battlefield attached.
3. **March of the Machines is sacrificed** to Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked, so noncreature artifacts (including this Aura) stop being creatures and it can legally remain attached ([Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3] is what would otherwise unattach and bin an Aura that is a creature).
4. **Activating the gained Transreliquat ability** targeting Deep Freeze is legal — Deep Freeze is an artifact thanks to Mycosynth Lattice. Sculpting Steel becomes a copy of Deep Freeze, except it keeps that copy ability. Because it changes what it copies while staying on the battlefield, no enters- or leaves-the-battlefield abilities trigger ([707.4]) — crucially, it never "leaves the battlefield," and it no longer *has* Animate Dead's "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it" ability at all. Gigantosaurus is therefore safe permanently, and it also loses the -1/-0.
5. **Immediately after that resolution** the Sculpting Steel is a Deep Freeze attached to Gigantosaurus (a legal "enchant creature"), so Gigantosaurus is briefly a 0/4 blue Wall with defender and no abilities ([Deep Freeze ruling #2] for the base-P/T overwrite, [613.1a] layer 1 for the copy effect being applied first).
6. **Enchantment Alteration** moves that Aura from Gigantosaurus (a creature) to another creature, Southern Elephant — legal, and the Aura gets a new timestamp ([701.3c]). Gigantosaurus reverts to a 10/10 Dinosaur with its normal abilities and stays on the battlefield. Southern Elephant is now enchanted by both the original Deep Freeze and the Sculpting Steel copy; both set base power/toughness 0/4, grant defender, remove other abilities, and add blue and Wall, so the later timestamp just re-applies the same values: a 0/4 blue Elephant Wall with defender.

Alison's original Animate Dead on Great-Horn Krushok is untouched throughout. Note that the granted "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura" wording refers only to that specific object ([201.5b], [201.5a]), which is irrelevant once the Aura is a Deep Freeze.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming March of the Machines was already sacrificed before the copy-Deep Freeze activation, as written. If instead March of the Machines were still on the battlefield when the Aura tried to exist, the Aura would be a creature, be unattached by state-based action, and be put into the graveyard ([Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3]) — and Animate Dead's leave-the-battlefield trigger would then have sacrificed Gigantosaurus.

Player count: Eureka has each player take turns putting permanents onto the battlefield in turn order ([101.4]), so with more than two players other players get their own Eureka puts, but none of that changes the outcome for Alison's permanents described above.

entries.question: Alex controls [Karametra, God of Harvests], and then casts [Opalescence]. Their devotion to white is 2. Is Karametra, God of Harvests a creature? If so, what is its power and toughness?

entries.answer:
Yes — Karametra, God of Harvests is a creature, and it's a 5/5 (a Legendary Enchantment Creature with no creature subtype).

Why:

1. Devotion. Karametra, God of Harvests checks your devotion to green and white, not devotion to white alone. Devotion counts colored mana symbols in the mana costs of permanents you control (CR 700.5a). Karametra, God of Harvests's own {3}{G}{W} contributes {G} and {W} (2), and Opalescence's {2}{W}{W} contributes 2 more — 4 total, well under seven (and even your stated devotion to white of 2 is under seven). So Karametra, God of Harvests's own ability is active.

2. Layer 4 (types), timestamp order (CR 613.1, 613.7). Karametra, God of Harvests's type-changing ability has the earlier timestamp (it was already on the battlefield); Opalescence's has the later one. Applying in order: first Karametra, God of Harvests stops being a creature and loses the creature type God (Karametra ruling #15), leaving a Legendary Enchantment; then Opalescence makes each other non-Aura enchantment a creature in addition to its other types — Karametra, God of Harvests qualifies, so it becomes a creature again. It does not get the God subtype back. Neither effect depends on the other (CR 613.8a isn't met — Karametra, God of Harvests's ability is driven by devotion, which is calculated before type-changing effects per CR 700.5a), so pure timestamp order governs.

3. Layer 7b (setting P/T). Opalescence sets its base power and toughness each equal to its mana value. Karametra, God of Harvests's mana value is 5 ({3}{G}{W}), so its printed 6/7 is overwritten and it is 5/5 (CR 208.4b, 613.4a, 302.4c).

Timing note: this assumes Karametra, God of Harvests was on the battlefield first (as stated), giving Opalescence the later timestamp. If Opalescence had the earlier timestamp, Karametra, God of Harvests's ability would apply last in layer 4 and it would not be a creature — and as a noncreature permanent it would have no power or toughness at all (CR 208.3), even though Opalescence's layer 7b part would still have started applying (CR 613.6 / Opalescence ruling #3).

Player count doesn't matter here: devotion counts only permanents Alex controls, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game (other players' enchantments are affected by Opalescence too, but that doesn't change Karametra, God of Harvests).

entries.question: Aaron equips [Skullclamp] onto [Champion of the Flame]. Does Champion of the Flame die?

entries.question: In their first main phase, Alexandra activates [Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance] to create two tokens, and Nehemiah responds with [Dress Down]. What happens with the tokens?

The two tokens are still created, and they keep haste.

The part that matters is the haste. Because the channel ability of Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance grants haste at the moment it resolves — after Dress Down entered — the tokens retain haste until end of turn and can attack this turn.

Under the other possible ordering (the channel ability of Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance fully resolves first, tokens made and granted haste, and only then Dress Down resolves), the tokens would lose haste, since haste would already be on them when Dress Down applies.

Dress Down is sacrificed at the beginning of the end step, per its own text. This analysis is the same regardless of the number of players; if several players had simultaneous choices, APNAP order would apply (rules 101.4, 616.1f), but nothing here requires that.

Also note tokens that ever leave the battlefield cease to exist as a state-based action (rules 111.7, 704.5d) — not relevant unless they die.

They're created as 1/1s and then gain haste. They'll be able to attack this turn.

entries.question: Aubree casts [Blood Moon]. Nikolas activates [Inkmoth Nexus]'s ability in response. What will Inkmoth Nexus look like after everything resolves? What will it look like next turn?

entries.answer:

Its name stays Inkmoth Nexus and no supertype is added — Blood Moon doesn't touch names or supertypes and doesn't make it basic [Blood Moon ruling #1].

Note the mana it taps for changed: it now produces {R} (one red mana), not {C} (colorless), and {C} is never interchangeable with colored or generic mana. Also, since it's a creature this turn, summoning-sickness rules apply — it can attack or tap for mana only if Nikolas has controlled it continuously since his most recent turn began [Inkmoth Nexus ruling #1].

Next turn: the animation effect was "until end of turn," so it wears off in the cleanup of this turn. With Blood Moon still on the battlefield, Inkmoth Nexus is just a nonbasic Land — Mountain named Inkmoth Nexus with "{T}: Add {R}" and nothing else — not a creature, no flying/infect, no {C} mana ability, and its {1} animation ability is gone, so Nikolas can't animate it again while Blood Moon remains [Blood Moon ruling #2].

This analysis is the same regardless of how many players are at the table; Blood Moon affects all nonbasic lands, not just an opponent's.

entries.question: Niko controls [Urza's Saga] on chapter 2. Ainsley casts [Magus of the Moon]. What happens to Urza's Saga?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Magus of the Moon makes Urza's Saga lose its chapter abilities while still a Saga, causing it to be immediately sacrificed as a state-based action.
entries.answer:
Urza's Saga is immediately sacrificed by Niko. Magus of the Moon makes all nonbasic lands Mountains, which strips Urza's Saga of its rules text — including its chapter abilities and any ability it gained from chapters I and II. The official ruling on Urza's Saga covers exactly this: "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed" [Urza's Saga ruling #1]. This is a state-based action, so it happens as soon as Magus of the Moon resolves and no player gets a chance to respond; it doesn't use the stack [704.5s], [714.4].

Details and assumptions:
- Timing: I'm assuming Magus of the Moon actually resolves. While Magus of the Moon is merely on the stack, nothing happens to Urza's Saga — Niko can still activate the {T}: Add {C} ability from chapter I or the {2}, {T} Construct-token ability from chapter II in response, and can do so at the last moment before Magus of the Moon resolves.
- Urza's Saga would normally keep abilities granted by chapters I and II for as long as it's on the battlefield [Urza's Saga ruling #5], but Magus of the Moon's type-changing effect removes them along with everything else in its text box; Magus of the Moon's own text overrides that general expectation.
- Because Urza's Saga is sacrificed before it ever reaches chapter III, its search-your-library chapter III ability never triggers.
- Note that Magus of the Moon affects nonbasic lands controlled by every player, so this is the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer — any player's Urza's Saga (or other chapter-bearing Saga that is a land) is sacrificed by its own controller [Magus of the Moon ruling #1].

entries.answer_gold:
It becomes an Enchantment Land - Saga Mountain with an ability to tap for {R}, an ability to tap for {C}, an ability to create Constructs, and no other abilities.

Because it has lost all of its chapter abilities while still being a Saga, it is immediately sacrificed the next time state-based actions are checked, per the Urza's Saga ruling "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed". Magus of the Moon has the same effect here as Blood Moon, which that ruling names explicitly.

entries.question: Nico controls [Dress Down], and Aya activates [Inkmoth Nexus]. What does it look like?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling — Inkmoth Nexus ends up a 1/1 artifact creature Blinkmoth with flying and infect and no mana ability, with Dress Down applied earlier by timestamp.
entries.answer:
Aya's Inkmoth Nexus becomes a 1/1 colorless Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature land that DOES have flying and infect. Nico's Dress Down does not strip them.

Why: this is the layer system (CR 613) doing timestamp bookkeeping.
- Layer 4 (types): the Inkmoth Nexus ability resolves and makes it an artifact creature (still a land) with subtypes Phyrexian Blinkmoth.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Dress Down's "Creatures lose all abilities" applies first because its timestamp is earlier — at that moment Inkmoth Nexus loses everything, including the {T}: Add {C} ability and the {1} animation ability itself. Then the animation effect, with the later timestamp, applies in layer 6 and grants flying and infect. An effect that has already begun applying in an earlier layer keeps applying in every later applicable layer even though the ability that generated it was removed in the meantime (CR 613.6, illustrated in the tool trace).
- Layer 7b: the same animation effect sets power/toughness to 1/1.

So the end result is a 1/1 artifact creature land with flying and infect, and no mana ability (the {T}: Add {C} was removed by Dress Down and nothing gave it back). Note infect means its combat damage to creatures is -1/-1 counters and to players is poison counters.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming Dress Down was already on the battlefield when Aya activated Inkmoth Nexus. If instead Nico casts (with flash) and resolves Dress Down after the animation ability has resolved, Dress Down would have the later timestamp, apply second in layer 6, and Inkmoth Nexus would be a 1/1 artifact creature land with no abilities at all — still 1/1, since the P/T setting happens in layer 7b regardless.

Player count doesn't matter here: this works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table, since Dress Down affects all creatures, not just an opponent's. (One multiplayer caveat from the provided rules: in a format with limited range of influence, an ability only sees objects within its controller's range — CR 801.11 — but ordinary multiplayer Commander has unlimited range, so Dress Down still hits Aya's Inkmoth Nexus.)

entries.answer_gold: It's a 1/1 Blinkmoth Land Artifact Creature with flying and infect, but no ability to tap for mana. The ability-changing effects are applied in the order they were created, so since Inkmoth Nexus's is more recent, it's applied last.

entries.question: Ariana controls [Painter's Servant] naming "blue." Nico casts [Dress Down]. What color are Painter's Servant and Dress Down?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Painter's Servant's layer-5 color-setting effect makes both permanents blue and Dress Down's layer-6 ability-stripping does not remove that color, so they reach the same ruling.
entries.answer:
Both Painter's Servant and Dress Down are blue.

Why: Painter's Servant's color-setting effect is applied in layer 5 (color-changing effects), while Dress Down's "Creatures lose all abilities" is applied in layer 6 (ability-adding/removing). Layers are applied in order (CR 613.1e), so Painter's Servant's ability is still present and applies its effect in layer 5 before layer 6 strips it, and once an effect has started to apply it keeps applying to that same set of objects. So every card, spell, and permanent — including Painter's Servant itself and Dress Down — is blue in addition to its other colors.

- Painter's Servant: printed mana cost {2}, so it's normally colorless (CR 202.2a). Painter's Servant's ability makes it blue, and since it's normally colorless it is simply blue, not blue-and-colorless (Painter's Servant ruling #0, ruling #5).
- Dress Down: mana cost {1}{U}, so it's blue already (CR 202.2a); adding blue changes nothing. It's blue.

Note on other effects: a later effect that outright *sets* an object's color (rather than adding one) would overwrite the blue from Painter's Servant (CR 105.3, Painter's Servant ruling #4). Dress Down doesn't do that — it only removes abilities, which is a layer-6 effect.

Timing/ordering: this holds regardless of whether Dress Down resolved before or after Painter's Servant entered, because layer order, not timestamp, governs across different layers here. The only thing that would change is going forward — once Dress Down's static ability is on the battlefield and Painter's Servant is a creature with no abilities, a *newly* entering Painter's Servant still couldn't choose a color if its ETB choice were removed first; but the already-established layer-5 effect continues.

Player count doesn't matter: nothing here depends on the number of opponents, so the answer is the same at a two-player table and in multiplayer.

entries.answer_gold: They will both be blue. Painter's Servant's color-changing effect is applied in layer 5 and Dress Down's ability-removing effect is applied later in layer 6, so Painter's Servant's ability has already been applied to the game state by the time its removed.

entries.question: Anabella controls [Blood Moon] and enchants their [Sunlit Marsh] with [Urban Utopia]. What colors can it tap for?
entries.reason: Both conclude that Blood Moon makes Sunlit Marsh a Mountain while Urban Utopia grants it "{T}: Add one mana of any color," so the land can tap for any single color.
entries.answer:
Sunlit Marsh can tap for any one color: {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G} (one mana of your choice each time you tap it).

Why: Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Sunlit Marsh is nonbasic, so in the type-changing layer it loses the Plains and Swamp subtypes and becomes just a Mountain, and it loses its other abilities, gaining the intrinsic Mountain ability "{T}: Add {R}" (CR 305.6, CR 107.4a; Blood Moon rulings #1 and #2). That kills its printed "{T}: Add {W} or {B}" — Sunlit Marsh keeps its name and any supertypes, but is not a basic land.

Urban Utopia grants the enchanted land "{T}: Add one mana of any color," and per Urban Utopia's ruling it doesn't change land types. Since the Aura was attached after Blood Moon was already applying (the timing I'm assuming from the question — Blood Moon first, then the Aura), its ability-granting effect has the later timestamp and applies on top of Blood Moon's ability removal. Running the layer system gives final abilities: "{T}: Add {R}" and "{T}: Add one mana of any color."

So Sunlit Marsh has two mana abilities, but it can only be tapped for one mana at a time; practically, it produces any single color you choose (the {R} ability is redundant). Note the color of mana produced is chosen on resolution, and if a mana ability could only produce an undefined type it would produce nothing (CR 106.5) — not an issue here, since "any color" is always defined among the five colors (CR 105.1).

Timing caveat: if Urban Utopia had been attached to Sunlit Marsh before Blood Moon entered the battlefield, Blood Moon's later ability-removing effect would strip the granted ability too, and Sunlit Marsh would tap only for {R}.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.
